Colt
KOHLT
noun
From the Saxon colt, the young of the horse or ass kind; rendering the Hebrew 'ayir, a young male ass, and the Greek polos, a foal — the beast on which the King of Zion rode into His city.

Biblical Definition

The colt is the young ass, and Scripture makes it the mount of the promised King. The blessing of Judah in Gen 49:11 binds “his ass’s colt unto the choice vine” — an image of such abundance that a man may tether a beast where the fruit grows — and Zechariah takes up the same line: “Rejoice greatly, O daughter of Zion… behold, thy King cometh unto thee: he is just, and having salvation; lowly, and riding upon an ass, and upon a colt the foal of an ass” (Zec 9:9). Every word there is deliberate. He is just; He has salvation; and He is lowly. A conqueror came on a war-horse. The King of Zion came on the colt of a working beast, and the humility is not a lapse from the majesty but the form the majesty took. Matthew records the fulfilment in the very words of the prophet (Mat 21:5), and John after Him (Joh 12:15). Two further details preach. The colt was one “whereon never man sat” (Luk 19:30; Mar 11:2) — what is consecrated to God must be unused by common service — and an unbroken colt carried Him quietly through a shouting crowd, which the creation does for its Maker. And He came riding on a borrowed beast, loosed at His word, to a city that would cry Hosanna on the Sunday and Crucify on the Friday. The King came lowly, and was received exactly as lowly kings are.

Webster 1828 Definition

The young of the horse or ass; in prophecy and fulfilment the beast on which the King of Zion rode lowly into His city.

COLT, the young of the horse or of the ass kind.

From the Saxon colt; Hebrew 'ayir; Greek polos, a foal.

Bound to the choice vine in the blessing of Judah (Gen 49:11).

Foretold as the mount of the coming King in Zec 9:9.

Fulfilled in the entry into Jerusalem (Mat 21:5; Joh 12:15).

Key Scripture

Gen 49:11 — "Binding his foal unto the vine, and his ass's colt unto the choice vine; he washed his garments in wine, and his clothes in the blood of grapes:"

Zec 9:9 — "Rejoice greatly, O daughter of Zion; shout, O daughter of Jerusalem: behold, thy King cometh unto thee: he is just, and having salvation; lowly, and riding upon an ass, and upon a colt the foal of an ass."

Mat 21:5 — "Tell ye the daughter of Sion, Behold, thy King cometh unto thee, meek, and sitting upon an ass, and a colt the foal of an ass."

Joh 12:15 — "Fear not, daughter of Sion: behold, thy King cometh, sitting on an ass's colt."

Modern Corruption

The lowly colt is made a lesson in humble leadership technique, and the triumphal entry a piece of political theatre, when it is a prophecy kept to the letter.

expand to see more

Two reductions run alongside each other. The first turns Zec 9:9 into a management principle: the King rode a donkey, therefore leaders should be approachable. The second, more corrosive, treats the entry as staged street theatre, a deliberate anti-imperial gesture crafted by a religious teacher for effect. Both leave out the one thing the Gospels insist on, that this was prophecy fulfilled — written five hundred years before by Zechariah, and before that pointed at in the blessing of Judah, and carried out to the letter down to the colt whereon never man sat. Matthew does not present it as a gesture. He quotes the prophet, and says it was done that it might be fulfilled.

The lowliness is therefore doctrine, not style. He is just, and He has salvation, and He is lowly, all in one verse; the humility of the colt does not qualify the kingship, it displays the kind of King He is — one who comes to bear a cross before He takes a crown. And it is deliberately not the whole picture, for the same Christ is seen in Rev 19 upon a white horse, in righteousness judging and making war. The first coming was on a colt; the second will not be. To take the lowliness of the entry as the whole of His character is to mistake the hour for the Person.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The young ass — bound to the choice vine in Judah’s blessing, and the mount of the King who came lowly to Zion.

expand to see more

Colt — Saxon colt; Hebrew 'ayir, a young ass; Greek polos, a foal.

Gen 49:11 binds the ass’s colt to the choice vine in the blessing of Judah.

Zec 9:9 foretells the King, just, having salvation, and lowly, upon a colt.

Mat 21:5 and Joh 12:15 record the fulfilment at the entry into Jerusalem.

Luk 19:30 and Mar 11:2: a colt whereon never man sat — consecrated, and quiet under its Maker.

Usage

"A conqueror came on a war-horse; the King of Zion came on a colt."

"“Whereon never man sat” — what is consecrated to God is kept from common use."

"The first coming was on a colt; the second is on a white horse."
